source_text: Quaeritis ergo necessitatem rei, quae esse non potest si patitur necessitatem. Huic motui animi libero, sine coactu originis inquieto, si causa ipso motu detur antiquior, non gignitur omnino, sed tollitur. Nomen enim ipsum voluntatis nullam vim habet alteram, quam non debere materiae quod movetur. Cum ergo unde orta sit voluntas, ipsa voluntate quaeris antiquius; non exordium eius, sed exitium requiris; omnino enim non intellegitur esse, si aut tenebris deputetur, aut nihilo; nec potest dici iam voluntas, quae subsistere non potest, nisi in motu animi, cogente nullo. Si ergo cogat aliquis, est quidem motus; sed non est voluntas, cuius vim illa definitionis pars secunda complevit, id est, nullo cogente. Si ergo voluntas nihil est aliud, quam motus animi, cogente nullo; male prorsus quaeritur origo rei, cuius conditio, si praevenitur, interit. Expende ergo quid sit quod roges: Unde, inquis, ipsa voluntas mala quasi arbor mala in primo homine potuit exoriri? [n80] , qui confiteris voluntatem de origine contigisse. Voluntas enim motus est animi, cogente nullo. Naturalia cuncta cogunt esse quod sequitur: voluntas autem si praecedentibus causis cogatur, voluntas esse mox desinit, et perdit conditionem, si accepit originem.
pass_a_gloss: You therefore ask a necessity of a thing which cannot be if it suffers necessity. To this free motion of the mind, restless without a coercion of origin, if a cause more ancient than the motion itself is given, it is not generated at all, but is taken away. For the name itself of will has no other force than that what is moved ought not to matter. When therefore you ask from where will arose something more ancient than will itself; you do not seek its beginning, but its destruction; for it is altogether not understood to be, if it is assigned either to darkness or to nothing; nor can that already be called will which cannot subsist except in a motion of the mind, no one compelling. If therefore someone compels, there is indeed a motion; but there is not will, whose force that second part of the definition completed, that is, no one compelling. If therefore will is nothing other than a motion of the mind, no one compelling; the origin of a thing is altogether badly asked, whose condition, if it is anticipated, perishes. Weigh therefore what it is that you ask: From where, you say, could the evil will itself as an evil tree arise in the first human?, you who confess that will happened from origin. For will is a motion of the mind, no one compelling. All natural things compel that to be which follows: but will, if it is compelled by preceding causes, immediately ceases to be will, and loses its condition, if it received an origin.

pass_b_english: You therefore seek a necessity behind something that cannot exist if it is subject to necessity. If a cause older than the movement itself is assigned to this free movement of the mind, active without compulsion from its origin, the will is not produced at all: it is removed. The very name ‘will’ means nothing other than that the movement does not owe its occurrence to matter. Therefore, when you ask where the will arose, seeking something older than the will itself, you seek not its beginning but its destruction. It cannot be understood to exist if it is attributed either to darkness or to nothing. Nor can that be called will which can exist only as a movement of the mind under no compulsion. If someone compels it, there is indeed a movement, but no will. The will’s force is completed by the definition’s second part: ‘under no compulsion.’ If will is nothing other than a movement of the mind under no compulsion, it is entirely wrong to ask the origin of a thing whose defining condition perishes if something precedes it. Weigh, then, what you ask: ‘Whence could the evil will itself, like an evil tree, arise in the first human being?’ (Augustine, Marriage and Desire 2.28.48). In asking this you confess that will came about through an origin. But will is a movement of the mind under no compulsion. All natural causes compel what follows to exist. If will is compelled by preceding causes, it immediately ceases to be will: by receiving such an origin, it loses its defining condition.

choices.why: Julian's definition of sin is an act of will. Keep 'will' rather than later 'free will' system language unless liberum arbitrium is present.
Julian's Manichaean charge: an evil that is a nature, not a will's act.
Julian's charge against Augustine: treating evil as a nature rather than as will.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
